items.summary: A Straits Times news analysis examines whether Anthropic's upcoming Nasdaq listing will confirm investor appetite for artificial intelligence or signal growing caution about its valuations. The company, founded in 2021 and based in San Francisco, develops the Claude family of AI models used for writing, software development, research and data analysis. Its Nov 19 IPO seeks a valuation of up to US$1.4 trillion (S$1.8 trillion), offering 825 million shares at between US$70 and US$78 apiece, potentially raising US$64.4 billion including shares sold by existing shareholders, which could make it the biggest IPO in history. A strong debut would signal that investors still see fortunes to be made from AI; a lacklustre one might suggest they are becoming more discerning about prices, and any subsequent fall in Anthropic's share price could indicate either broader loss of confidence or reassessment of its valuation. The analysis notes this need not be negative: given the transformational potential of AI, a correction could offer an opportunity for long-term value investors to enter the market. Anthropic plans to use proceeds from the offering and a concurrent US$26 billion private placement to fund general corporate purposes including computing infrastructure investments, research and development, and business expansion. Its prospectus points to applications ranging from accelerating scientific discoveries and helping researchers tackle diseases such as cancer, to improving productivity in public and private sectors; for example, AI could help doctors identify diseases earlier while businesses use it to improve efficiency and reduce costs. The strategic importance of the technology is also evident: on Nov 16 Washington announced new restrictions requiring US export licences for shipments of certain advanced AI chips to data centres in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand and Indonesia among other countries, seeking to prevent Chinese companies from accessing American computing power through overseas facilities following reporting that the Commerce Department turned a blind eye to smuggling of advanced Nvidia chips to China. The prospectus also lays bare substantial costs and risks: Anthropic is still unprofitable, recording a net loss of US$104 billion for the first nine months of the year compared with US$25.1 billion in the same period in 2025; it has disclosed approximately US$900.9 billion in purchase and lease commitments, much related to computing capacity extending over many years, raising questions about whether the company can sustain growth while generating sufficient profits. The analysis draws parallels with past bubbles: during the late-1990s dotcom boom investors poured money into internet companies on assumptions of transformative potential; while they were right about the technology's promise, many were wrong about the companies and prices, losing fortunes betting on it. Similarly, the cryptocurrency boom attracted investors with promises of decentralised finance and attractive returns but encouraged speculation, excessive leverage and hype; the collapse of TerraUSD stablecoin and its sister token Luna in May 2022 triggered heavy losses, deepened by November's implosion of FTX exchange whose founder Sam Bankman-Fried was convicted of fraud and sentenced to 25 years. The analysis cautions that while AI is generating substantial commercial revenue and delivering practical benefits across industries, the danger remains another speculative bubble; when expectations eventually disappoint a sharp correction could erode confidence in the entire sector including companies with sound business models, causing a setback for innovation even if underlying potential remains intact. It notes greater scrutiny following a Democratic sweep in the US midterms would pressure AI companies to exercise financial discipline and demonstrate sustainable profits while encouraging investors to pay closer attention to safety and corporate governance given failures could have far-reaching consequences. Nvidia is cited as a reminder of why governance matters: its market value grew more than tenfold from end-2022 to its peak in October 2026 under co-founder Jensen Huang, but his abrupt resignation in November exposed risks of a company so closely identified with one individual without a publicly known successor; Nvidia has since lost about US$1.8 trillion in market value amid concerns over AI valuations and leadership uncertainty, showing that even strong earnings cannot insulate against governance questions. The piece concludes that while AI may change the world for the better, investors should not necessarily pay any price for a stake in its future.
items.title: Anthropic's IPO: Singapore investors weigh AI promise against bubble risk

Asian shares rose on Nov 18 after Nvidia posted a better-than-expected sales forecast, snapping four consecutive days of regional losses. MSCI's broadest Asia-Pacific index outside Japan advanced 0.9%, led by South Korea's KOSPI gaining as much as 3.3%. Japan's Nikkei 225 climbed 0.6%, while US S&P 500 e-mini futures were up 0.5%.

Nvidia shares rose 4.7% in after-hours trading, reporting quarterly revenue above forecasts in its first earnings report since Jensen Huang's abrupt departure as CEO in November. The gains came despite the Wall Street Journal reporting that the SEC is probing Nvidia over recent turmoil.

Jake Behan, head of capital markets at Direxion in New York, said: "I've looked at this whole week as a referendum on AI." He added that Anthropic was about to give investors a read on appetite for the next generation of AI companies. Overnight, Wall Street stocks sold off again with the S&P 500 down 1% before Nvidia's report.

Oil prices edged lower, with Brent crude futures 0.2% below US$93 a barrel as Asian trading began. The benchmark rebounded from Nov 17 declines amid worries about continuing tanker attacks in the Strait of Hormuz and expectations of falling US crude inventories against projected supply surplus from recovering Middle East exports.

Westpac analysts noted: "Risk sentiment remained firmly on the defensive overnight, with the tech-led sell-off extending across global markets." The next major AI industry health check would come as Anthropic prepared to price its shares later Nov 18 ahead of a market debut that could value the company at up to US$1.4 trillion (S$1.8 trillion), per Bloomberg News.

The yen was 0.1% weaker against the dollar at 159.49, while Japan's exports rose for a 14th successive month in October on semiconductor-related demand. The US dollar index climbed 0.1% to 103.66, reaching its highest level since April 2, 2025 — the date of Trump's Liberation Day tariff announcement.

The yield on the US 10-year Treasury rose 2.2 basis points to 5.123%. On Nov 17, St. Louis Fed president Alberto Musalem said the Federal Reserve may need several rate hikes to control inflation and should act soon. In cryptocurrencies, bitcoin was up 0.9% at US$64,862.82 while ether rose 1.0% at US$1,823.74.
items.title: Asia stocks rebound on Nvidia beat as Anthropic IPO looms

items.summary: Nvidia reported on Tuesday that its equity stake in private companies is now worth $65.5 billion, up from the $22 billion it had reported in January. The increase reflects both new investments and significant markups of existing portfolio companies. In the past quarter alone, Nvidia invested $16 billion into equities, while spending $58 billion over the prior nine months of its fiscal year; this figure includes purchases of shares in public and private companies. For comparison, in November 2025 the company reported spending only $5 billion buying equity during the first nine months of that fiscal year, underscoring how much larger these bets were relative to last year. Nvidia stated in late 2023 that its corporate investing aims to expand the AI ecosystem by backing startups it considers “game changers and market makers.” Over nearly three years afterward, PitchBook reported that the chipmaker had invested in nearly 350 startups. Those include Anthropic and OpenAI; neolabs such as Thinking Machines and Reflection; neoclouds like Lambda, Nscale, and Crusoe; plus other companies developing AI infrastructure, robotics, and applications. Nvidia has also become a major financier of data center construction, reporting $118 billion in guarantees, with $105 billion serving as the backstop for OpenAI's $500 billion data center project in Ohio. These commitments were funded by allocating a meaningful portion of excess cash flows. During Tuesday's earnings call, Kress said Nvidia would continue providing financing assistance to strong customers but added that “as the market matures and additional sources of capital become available,” it would be “rigorously evaluating future investments, commitments, and guarantees.” A central question for the venture ecosystem is whether this growth can continue under interim CEO Kress and Jensen Huang's successor. Huang's extensive dealmaking has reportedly concerned Kress, and investors told TechCrunch that they expect her to adopt a more conservative approach—being more selective with new investments and writing smaller checks into existing portfolio companies. Nvidia also stated its intent “to return all excess free cash flow net of strategic uses to shareholders during this last quarter and going forward.” Just how active startup backing will be under Kress's leadership, and under the future permanent CEO, remains uncertain; for now, venture capitalists are bracing for a meaningful pullback in capital.
items.title: Nvidia's startup stakes ballooned to $65B, but Huang's exit puts future deals in doubt

items.summary: During Nvidia's first earnings call since CEO Jensen Huang resigned, interim CEO Colette Kress reaffirmed the company's commitment to open source AI. She stated that Nvidia remains dedicated to fostering an open model ecosystem so every country, company, and industry can build its own intelligence, adding that open models are accelerating AI adoption. Citing OpenRouter data, she noted a 35-fold year-over-year surge in weekly token volume on the platform, including a 3.5-fold increase over the past three months. Kress also addressed Nvidia's planned acquisition of Hugging Face for $12.9 billion — agreed to in September and described as its second-largest deal ever. The platform serves more than 18 million developers and 200,000 companies, and remains on track to join Nvidia despite Huang's departure. Huang had been a strong advocate for open source AI; his ouster prompted Hugging Face's CEO to call it "a sad day" while promising to fight harder for the cause. So far, Nvidia has not directly addressed its Hugging Face plans during the Q&A portion of the call, though Kress said together they will scale the platform and make intelligence more open, capable, and accessible. Huang resigned as CEO last week amid reports of extramarital affairs — including one with Alice Huang, an executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed suspected of being a Chinese spy — plus accusations involving two direct reports; he is set to testify before Congress by Thanksgiving. The SEC is also investigating Nvidia over whether its disclosures misled investors, per the WSJ. Within Nvidia, Huang had pushed for the Nemotron family of open-weight models built for long-running agentic AI and reasoning workloads. On the call, Kress said Nemotron is now the most widely used U.S. open model on OpenRouter and where developers start building their own intelligence, describing it as a foundation empowering the ecosystem.
items.title: Nvidia reaffirms open source AI commitment after Jensen Huang's exit

At Microsoft's Ignite 2026 keynote, the company introduced two new frontier AI models designed for everyday coding tasks. The lead model, MAI Code 2, reportedly delivers 96% of Claude Opus 5.5 performance at just 5% of its cost. A companion Flash variant is positioned as comparable to lower-end GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5 models, also at considerably reduced pricing. Microsoft frames these claims using usage-based API metrics rather than subscription tiers; the company explicitly notes that paying customers on $100/month plans would not automatically receive equivalent performance for a fraction of the price.

The broader strategic narrative centers on reducing dependence on OpenAI and Anthropic. Despite its multi-billion-dollar investment in OpenAI dating back to 2023, Microsoft is now benchmarking internally built models against external providers and offering them as optional choices within GitHub Copilot (1658-1670), Microsoft 365, and Fabric. CEO Satya Nadella emphasized AI's centrality across the company's operations.

Microsoft also announced MAI Work Flash, derived from Code 2 Flash, which extends capabilities to non-coding productivity tasks including generating Excel formulas, working with Word documents, tracking decisions in Teams, and reformatting PowerPoint presentations. The article notes that coding agents serve as effective training grounds for work-focused agentic tools because code output is highly measurable.

The piece presents hypothetical cost projections: a company spending $0.01 per AI request could reduce this to $0.001 per request with these models, potentially dropping daily inference costs from $1 million to about $100,000 and saving roughly $325 million annually.

The article raises important caveats: Microsoft reports figures using a 50% introductory discount (4705-4708), which is why the analysis uses $0.001 per request rather than $0.0005 (4762-4768). Benchmark selection could involve cherry-picking, though the author expresses doubt that Microsoft significantly inflates numbers since it benefits more from these models than its customers. The company also acknowledged these models are not designed for challenging agentic or research workloads but performed unusually well on visualization assignments.
items.title: Microsoft Unveils Cheaper AI Coding Models at Ignite 2026 Keynote

items.summary: The Compute Platform team at Databricks provisions virtual machines and coordinates cluster creation across AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud for classic compute workloads. Historically they protected the system with fixed API request-rate limits—accepting a set number of requests per time window—which worked when available capacity and per-request work were predictable but became hard to tune as workload mix and dependency failures grew. Conservative limits rejected customer requests even during spare capacity, yet still accepted them while dependencies slowed; engineers manually lowered and raised the limits around incidents. The team replaced this with adaptive concurrency control: a slot-based limit on active cluster-creation workflows that expands when capacity is available and contracts under congestion signals like provisioning latency or thread-pool saturation, keeping a fixed API request-rate ceiling as a final guardrail against exceptionally high incoming traffic. They explain the difference using a kitchen analogy—a fixed rule of ten new orders per minute turns away work despite spare cooks and keeps accepting it faster than an oven can finish meals, whereas tracking in-progress meals with adjustable slots lets fewer start when capacity falls and more begin as it recovers. A single API call only validates and records a request before returning; the actual provisioning—validating dependencies, updating state, and launching VMs—runs asynchronously for minutes while the handler completes in milliseconds, so one request can provision many VMs and its duration depends on dependency health. During shared slowdowns more workflows take longer simultaneously, leaving far more work in flight at the same incoming rate; when a dependency degrades, retries from accepted work pile onto it, causing further failures and yet more retries—a retry storm that persists after traffic normalizes because request-rate limits do not see internal retries. A lower fixed rate only buys headroom by rejecting healthy-period work, while raising it uses capacity better but accepts more during degradation; one number cannot cover both days. The team distinguishes two failure situations behind a 'too many requests' message: shared-dependency slowdowns where the customer's traffic is normal and asking them to change behavior misattributes a service problem, versus an unusually large burst from one tenant competing for resources while the service stays healthy—so they track system health, per-tenant demand, and scheduling decisions separately. For long-running operations that take minutes, queuing accepted requests with bounded wait times lets bursts drain rather than returning immediate errors followed by retries, provided waiting fits each request's deadline; an unbounded queue can turn a brief disruption into hours of delay, so they bound backlog size and expiration time, keep queued records small instead of running workers holding scarce resources, and plan for the worst-case backlog to discard cheaply. A scheduler also decides which work goes first under contention—balancing tenant shares with letting tenants use idle capacity while preserving fair access—and this choice shapes whether many customers each see one slow request or one customer sees many; a successful API response does not guarantee immediate launch or completion within fixed time. The initial rollout analysis reported 7.5× higher default cluster-creation request-rate limits, more than 99.99% fewer cluster-creation rate-limit errors in the reported scope, and removal of over a hundred customer-specific rate-limit overrides in scope; since then few customers have hit the higher limits and no new manual overrides were added for those limits. They note open design questions—weighted slots or separate limits when operations carry very different resource costs, where to apply control so one slow dependency does not hold up unrelated work—and that pairing concurrency limits with retry backoff and attempt caps reduces pressure during cloud-provider recovery; the controller counts active provisioning workflows only, not running clusters or allocated VMs and vCPUs. They also point readers to High Performance Ratelimiting at Databricks for enforcing API quotas at scale as a complementary problem.
items.title: How Databricks Raised Cluster Creation Rate Limits by 7.5× Using Adaptive Concurrency Control

items.summary: Google is replacing its Gemini feature 'Gems' with a new capability called 'Skills,' effective November 17, 2026. While the Gems interface itself is being retired, any existing Gems will not be lost; they automatically convert to Skills, though users may transfer them manually if they wish to begin using them immediately. Accessing the now-retiring Gems section requires going through Settings, where a message informs users that 'Starting November 17, 2026, we'll automatically begin migrating all of your Gems to Skills.' The cutoff date for accessing existing Gems is December 16, 2026; Workspace business, enterprise, and non-profit accounts will instead be cut off in March 2027, while Workspace education accounts are scheduled for a June 2027 cutoff. Functionally, a Gemini Skill operates much like a Gem: users describe the specific situations when Gemini should apply it automatically and specify what they want it to do, ideally with concrete examples of desired output. Google's own example involves a marketing team sharing a brand-voice skill that references their brand guidelines document in Drive, or a team lead sharing an onboarding skill based on the team handbook. The principal distinction is structural: whereas Gems were standalone chats, Skills are custom instructions that function within any conversation. Users may create as many Skills as they like, but only 100 can be active at once. Google has carried over two features from Gems to ease adoption of Skills. First, users can share a Skill with other people and choose whether the recipient may edit it or view it only; sharing is done via the three-bar menu in the top left > Customize > Skills, where permissions can also be viewed or changed. A caveat noted is that at present Skills can only be shared through the Gemini web app, not the mobile app. Second, when creating a Skill, users may include files up to 100MB from other Google products such as Drive, Photos, and Notebook, along with local device files; these are referenced every time the Skill runs and update in real time per Google's description. These file-sharing capabilities previously existed within Gems and are being moved into Skills so that the new feature is more comparable to its predecessor.
items.title: Google Retires Gemini Gems and Migrates to Skills Starting November 17, 2026

items.summary: Prime Minister Lawrence Wong announced his upcoming visit to China this week, first attending the APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting in Shenzhen and then visiting Beijing. He framed the trip around a shared appreciation of openness and engagement as an important foundation of Singapore-China relations, arguing that keeping countries' doors open is more important than ever amid growing global uncertainty and fragmentation. Wong highlighted Shenzhen's transformation from a small town into a global technology hub over just a few decades as evidence of China's reform and opening up, drawing a parallel to how openness shaped Singapore's own development despite its limited resources. He noted that the two countries' friendship predates diplomatic relations established in 1990, with earlier leaders including Mr Lee Kuan Yew and Mr Deng Xiaoping laying foundational ties built on mutual respect, trust and understanding; last year they commemorated 35 years of diplomatic relations. Wong described three government-to-government projects that illustrate the evolving partnership: the Suzhou Industrial Park to support industrial development, the Tianjin Eco-City to explore sustainable urban living, and more recently the Chongqing Connectivity Initiative focused on strengthening trade between western China and South-east Asia. He emphasized that each project reflected its time's opportunities and priorities, showing how cooperation has continually adapted with both sides learning from one another. Wong also noted that since their bilateral Free Trade Agreement came into force in 2009, it has been progressively upgraded to keep pace with changing needs, extending beyond traditional trade and investment into the digital economy, sustainability and innovation. Looking ahead, he pointed to China's 15th Five-Year Plan emphasizing high-quality development, innovation and improving people's livelihoods, alongside Singapore's completed Economic Strategy Review aimed at strengthening competitiveness through new technologies and good jobs; both face common challenges including rapid technological change, ageing populations, workforce skills needs, and the transition toward greener growth. Wong argued these shared challenges present opportunities for cooperation, particularly in applying artificial intelligence across industries and developing emerging technologies. He stressed that Singapore remains a firm supporter of an open, inclusive and rules-based economic architecture, believing regional cooperation should bring countries closer rather than divide them into competing blocs, even as he acknowledged governments' understandable responsibility to safeguard their economies against disruptions from rising geopolitical tensions and trade barriers. Wong noted Singapore's upcoming ASEAN chairmanship next year will focus on deepening regional integration and expanding cooperation with all partners including China, building on the ASEAN-China Free Trade Area whose latest upgrade covers digital and green economies, supply chain connectivity and innovation. He praised China's APEC theme of "Building an Asia-Pacific Community to Prosper Together" as timely given its focus on openness, innovation and cooperation, expressing Singapore's commitment to working with all APEC economies in Shenzhen and building on those efforts when Singapore chairs APEC in 2030. Wong concluded by reaffirming the All-Round High-Quality Future-Oriented Partnership between the two countries as reflecting both the breadth of their cooperation and a shared commitment to take it further, arguing that at a time of growing global divisions, strengthening connections rather than erecting barriers can help build a more resilient and prosperous Asia-Pacific. Wong's remarks were delivered in his capacity as Singapore's Prime Minister during an official visit tied to APEC participation; the article presents these views without independent verification or additional analysis beyond what he stated.
items.title: Singapore Prime Minister Lawrence Wong on Strengthening Singapore-China Relations Ahead of APEC Visit

items.summary:
Historically, resolving customer records to a person-based ID such as RampID required data teams to export PII to an external service, wait for a match file, and load results back in. Each step added a pipeline to maintain, a copy of sensitive data to govern, and delay before the results were usable. LiveRamp Embedded Identity on Databricks addresses this by bringing identity resolution into the customer's own environment through packaged clean rooms, so customer PII does not leave owned storage while analytics and AI workloads continue running in place under Unity Catalog governance. Packaged clean rooms remove that round-trip entirely: a resolved list of RampIDs is returned directly to the customer's environment as appended match keys for downstream use cases such as customer 360, audience building, activation, partner collaboration, and measurement.

The architecture centers on three components. The central clean room is a Databricks-managed environment separate from both the customer's and LiveRamp's workspaces, with no administrative access held by either company. OpenSharing—formerly Delta Sharing—is the open sharing protocol underlying Databricks Clean Rooms; neither party copies tables into the room, instead each adds Unity Catalog assets that grant the central clean room read-only access so it reads live current versions rather than stale extracts from a prior run. The connection leverages Databricks-to-Databricks sharing to preserve Unity Catalog governance on both sides: the provider controls which assets it exposes, the customer controls which tables it adds, and all sharing activity is audited for both parties. OpenSharing also carries more than tables—it can share models, unstructured data, JAR files, private libraries, python wheels, and more—which enables LiveRamp to deliver its full identity resolution service.

A packaged clean room extends privacy beyond the standard approval-based model in a way that suits a provider-customer relationship. In an approval-based Databricks clean room every collaborator is a peer: any party can add tabular or unstructured data and/or code, all parties must approve code before it runs, collaborators never see each other's raw data but do see the aliases of shared tables along with column names and types—fitting joint analysis such as two companies measuring audience overlap. Even there, privacy is partially preserved by packaging a volume so approvers review only the notebook that calls the library rather than the library itself. A packaged clean room instead extends privacy to the entire analysis for a different relationship: one party (LiveRamp) ships an analysis as a product and the other (the customer) runs it against its own data, with no approval step and neither party seeing the other's data assets at all—not even table names or schemas. The provider can offer the same package to many customers in separate clean rooms for scalable deployment.

For identity resolution specifically, this split protects both sides: LiveRamp's identity graph and matching logic remain its intellectual property and stay invisible to the customer, while the customer's PII and resolved results remain private to the customer. A single run writes to two schemas—both delivered via OpenSharing into catalogs specified at set-up, viewable in Catalog Explorer under Shares received—and both are queryable immediately; for long-term use beyond 30 days these tables must be copied down into the customer's own cloud storage.

Both parties can see every run's history including status, timing, and notebook. Because the customer owns the data and LiveRamp owns the code, neither side alone has the full picture when a run fails; the shared view of run status plus shared output schema lets both teams troubleshoot from the same facts without exposing data. Clean room activity is also recorded in each party's system tables (system.access.clean_room_events) for an audit trail.

To operate this, customers need a LiveRamp agreement with Identity API credentials, a Unity Catalog workspace, and the CREATE CLEAN ROOM privilege; they prepare an input table of PII touchpoints plus a metadata table holding their LiveRamp credentials and run settings in LiveRamp's documented format, then create the clean room from the LiveRamp tile under Identity Resolution Providers and choose a central clean room region. If storage sits behind a firewall or private endpoint, SecureConnect must be enabled first.

Billing falls to the creator of the clean room at Jobs Serverless rates for compute, which starts only per run so there is no idle environment to maintain. Packaged clean rooms thus turn identity resolution into something a data team runs rather than maintains—no exports to schedule, no match files to wait on, and no extra copies of PII to govern.

The article notes several boundaries: resolved tables are retained for 30 days before requiring copy-down; the customer alone triggers runs while both parties share run history and output schema only for logs and metrics that LiveRamp's code writes; LiveRamp's code does call its identity service to authenticate, governed by the clean room's egress network policy shown on the Security tab; and setup details are directed to external guides rather than provided in full. Full setup steps are referenced through LiveRamp's guide "Perform RampID identity resolution in Databricks" and the Databricks packaged clean rooms documentation.
items.title: Packaged Clean Rooms for RampID Identity Resolution on Databricks

items.summary: Waymo has temporarily suspended its driverless vehicles from operating on all US freeways, a decision the company attributes to a recent California DMV order. The California DMV banned Waymo's driverless taxis from state freeways following several traffic incidents and cited an "imminent hazard to public safety," pointing specifically to an incident this month in which multiple driverless Waymo vehicles entered an active construction zone on US Route 101 south of San Francisco, where construction workers, vehicles, and equipment are present. The DMV stated that the ban reflects a risk from recurring incursions by Waymo's vehicles into such active construction zones. A second incident earlier this month involved footage widely circulated on social media showing a Waymo vehicle attempting to overtake patrol vehicles deliberately slowing traffic on a San Francisco highway. California's DMV said its driverless taxis presented a risk "due to recurring incursions by its vehicles into active construction zones where construction workers, vehicles and equipment are present." The ban took effect on 11 November and will remain in place until Waymo demonstrates it has taken effective corrective actions addressing the deficiencies that led to the restrictions. In response, a Waymo spokesperson said: "In alignment with our safety-first principles, we have also temporarily restricted freeway operations across our other operating markets to evaluate our performance." The company added that it was working with state officials diligently and responsibly to resume freeway operations, noting no injuries or collisions were reported following the Route 101 incident. Waymo's driverless taxis can continue to operate on regular city streets in its current markets. Data on Waymo's website indicates its vehicles are involved in 95% fewer crashes resulting in serious injury compared to human drivers. Waymo currently operates driverless taxis in 15 US cities, though it offered freeway rides only in a handful of locations including San Francisco, Los Angeles, and Miami. The company previously recalled thousands of self-driving cars over a software issue that could allow vehicles to drive into flooded roads, an action taken in May; the same month saw multiple Waymo vehicles spotted driving around a cul-de-sac in Atlanta, Georgia, in the early hours of the morning. This article is based on untrusted source text and should be treated with appropriate caution regarding its accuracy and framing.
items.title: Waymo suspends driverless taxis from all US freeways after California ban

items.summary: Electric power tool brand Greenworks is expanding its battery-powered lineup significantly with the launch of OPTIMUS, an all-new go-anywhere electric side-by-side utility vehicle (SxS) that packs over 100 equivalent horsepower and a 40 mph top speed. First shown at Equip Exposition 2026 in Kentucky last month, the newly redesigned Greenworks OPTIMUS UTV is described as the biggest, baddest, and newest addition to the company's battery-backed commercial ecosystem. According to Yin Chen, CEO of Greenworks, 'OPTIMUS has always been about pushing battery power beyond what the industry expects,' positioning the vehicle as a natural extension of the brand's vision for bringing professionals more ways to put battery power to work across property maintenance equipment and supporting utility vehicles and charging systems. The OPTIMUS is built around Greenworks' 400V high-voltage electrical platform, which mates a pair of compact electric motors combining for 110 equivalent horsepower. Those motors draw power from a 19 kWh lithium-ion battery pack with enough efficiency to hit the 40 mph top speed and cover up to 68 miles of range under typical operating conditions. When hauling, OPTIMUS offers buyers a 2,500 lb towing capacity and 1,300 lb payload capacity along with 11 full inches of ground clearance and a beefy 6,000 lb electric winch. Independent suspension, oversized all-terrain tires, torque vectoring differentials, and multiple terrain modes round out the spec sheet for a machine designed to handle demanding off-road applications.
items.title: Greenworks launches OPTIMUS electric UTV with battery-forward commercial platform

items.summary: JAKSON Green Limited has announced the signing of definitive agreements to acquire a majority stake in Ocior Energy India Private Limited, described as a developer of green hydrogen, green ammonia, green methanol and other Power-to-X solutions. The acquisition is expected to strengthen JAKSON Green's presence in the emerging green hydrogen sector and expand its clean energy project portfolio across India, the Middle East and North Africa (MNFA). Both companies state that combining their capabilities aims to strengthen project development, improve execution capabilities, and support growing global demand for low-carbon fuels. Ocior Energy has developed a portfolio of utility-scale green hydrogen, green ammonia and green methanol projects at various stages of development, supported by renewable energy assets with opportunities across India and international markets, particularly the MNFA. One key project is its proposed 200,000 metric tonnes per annum (MTPA) green ammonia plant at Gopalpur, Odisha; Ocior has received a Letter of Award from the Solar Energy Corporation of India Limited (SECI), a Government of India enterprise, for supplying 85,000 MTPA of green ammonia, with an initial offtake period under the award of 10 years. In addition to its green ammonia development, Ocior is working on two green hydrogen projects, each with a proposed capacity of 5 kilotonnes per annum (KTPA), developed in Madhya Pradesh and Visakhapatnam, Andhra Pradesh; the hydrogen from these facilities is intended for supply to Bharat Petroleum Corporation Limited (BPCL) and Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Limited (HPCL), respectively. The acquisition will combine Ocior Energy's experience in developing green molecule projects with JAKSON Green's capabilities across independent power production (IPP), project development, engineering procurement and construction (EPC), and operations and maintenance (O&M). Bikesh Ogra, Vice Chairman and Global CEO of JAKSON Green, said the global energy transition is creating significant opportunities for green hydrogen and its derivatives, and that the acquisition would bring an established development platform and strong project pipeline to support building a globally integrated clean energy business. Ranjit Gupta, CEO of Ocior Energy, said the partnership would help accelerate project execution and expand the portfolio by combining resources, expertise and capabilities to support a competitive and sustainable hydrogen economy. The companies note demand for green hydrogen, ammonia and methanol continues to grow in domestic and international markets. No purchase price or financing terms were disclosed in the announcement; figures cited are described as proposed capacities under awards and letters of award rather than completed commitments.
items.title: JAKSON Green to Acquire Majority Stake in Ocior Energy

items.summary: America's largest weapons manufacturers face a January 1 Pentagon deadline requiring them to prove their magnets are free of Chinese rare earths, even though dysprosium and terbium—the two heavy rare earths used to keep powerful magnets working under extreme temperatures in fighter aircraft, missiles, and other advanced military equipment—are nearly entirely controlled by Beijing. China controls close to 100% of the processing for these metals. To address this dependency, Washington has proposed making 200 acres of a 43,000-acre Army depot in Utah available for REalloys (NASDAQ: ALOY) to build a heavy rare earth processing plant under a lease that could last up to 75 years. On November 3, REalloys and the U.S. Army signed a non-binding term sheet at Tooele Army Depot; REalloys would finance, construct, and operate the facility while the Army retains first opportunity to purchase its dysprosium and terbium production. The timing aligns with China's pause on expanded rare earth export controls, which Beijing extended two months to January 10, 2027—nine days after the Pentagon ban takes effect. Defense contractors have requested more time but Washington has kept the deadline in place. REalloys holds an advantage through its developing North American supply chain that converts rare earth oxides into metals; it is working with the Saskatchewan Research Council on what they describe as North America's first fully integrated commercial rare earth processing and metallization operation, while retired four-star General Jack Keane, a board member, warned China has made clear it is prepared to use this dependence as leverage. The Army lease would give REalloys long-term industrial presence on an American military installation with the Pentagon seeking first access; Waksman told Fox Business that the structure lets the Army expand the critical minerals industrial base without putting taxpayer dollars at risk, and CEO Lipi Sternheim said it puts part of the rare earth supply chain under military oversight. Keane called the term sheet 'an important step toward bringing heavy rare earth processing onto a U.S. defense installation.' The arrangement still requires REalloys and the Army to complete environmental review, permitting, and requirements before signing the final lease; the term sheet provides for a 50-year lease with a 25-year extension option, with REalloys paying fair-market rent plus participation rent once commercial operations begin. On processing capacity, magnet makers buy dysprosium and terbium as metal rather than oxide, and China ran nearly 100% of global heavy rare earth metallization until recently; outside China only a handful of plants make these metals—Less Common Metals in the U.K., the Korean Metals Plant at Ochang (which has made initial sales), and REalloys' Euclid, Ohio operation as the only North American heavy rare earth metallization capability. REalloys is scaling its $40 million plant built at SRC in Saskatoon before moving to Ohio; it will produce about 30 tonnes of dysprosium metal and 15 tonnes of terbium metal a year, with a provisional patent on a hydrofluoric acid-free fluorination process that could reduce capex, opex, and improve sustainability. REalloys holds rights to about 80% of SRC's expanded output—525 tonnes of NdPr metal, 30 tonnes of dysprosium oxide, and 15 tonnes of terbium oxide a year—and targets first NdPr metal from SRC in Q1 2027 with the dysprosium and terbium metallization plant commissioning in Q1 2028. items.summary: According to company proxy and corporate filings, former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang can nominate two directors to the Nvidia board ahead of the company's annual shareholder meeting and vote. This ability gives the co-founder a route to future influence on the AI chip leader following his resignation as CEO last week. Chip industry executives, investors and customers are scrutinizing Nvidia closely to understand what role Huang will play in the company after resigning. Under Nvidia's rules, any shareholder or group of shareholders that owns more than 3 per cent of the voting power for at least three years is entitled to nominate directors who will be included in the company's proxy materials and vote at its annual meeting, which typically takes place in June. Data from LSEG shows Huang and entities tied to him have owned more than 3 per cent of Nvidia's shares for more than three years; he currently owns roughly 3.5 per cent of the company. Any nominee would need to qualify as an independent member of the board, and candidates would go on Nvidia's proxy ballot. Nominating board members would not guarantee Huang's allies seats on the company board because shareholders would still need to vote to approve potential candidates; Nvidia may also leave a nominee out if the person has violated the company's bylaws and charter. On November 8, Nvidia's board said it initiated an investigation in light of recent reporting that Huang had been the target of a foreign intelligence effort, though Reuters could not determine whether Huang's conduct broke the company's bylaws or charter. Nvidia and a representative for Huang did not respond to requests for comment. Since Huang resigned from Nvidia last week following his extramarital affairs, executives such as Elon Musk, employees, investors and US President Donald Trump have advocated for his return to the top job at the chip designer; however, three people with knowledge of the matter told Reuters on Monday that the board was not considering reinstating Huang. Huang released a statement on Tuesday saying he 'would be honored' to return as CEO if the board decided such a move would be in the best interest of shareholders and employees. On Tuesday after the market close, Nvidia forecast quarterly revenue above Wall Street estimates, giving investors some relief after the uncertainty caused by Huang's exit.

items.summary: Amazon founder and CEO Jeff Bezos said he was "heavily involved" in casting actor Robert Pattinson as the next James Bond. Speaking at Semafor Silicon Valley & The World Event in California, Bezos described his original reaction to Pattinson—known for Batman and the Twilight franchise—as being "biased against" him because of his fame, noting that the role has typically gone to a less well-known actor at casting time. However, he said during screen tests it became clear that "it was so obvious he is James Bond." Bezos added, "There was something special about Rob," and described the decision as "immediately undebated," with director Denis Villeneuve and others gravitating toward Pattinson. This marks the first 007 film outside the creative control of the Broccoli family, who had overseen the franchise since its first Bond film in 1962; Amazon purchased MGM—which co-owns the franchise—in 2022. Pattinson was unveiled as the seventh James Bond on Monday, succeeding Daniel Craig, and will star in the 26th Bond movie due for release in 2028. In a statement, the London-born actor called it "the honour of a lifetime." The film will be directed by Denis Villeneuve, though its title and exact release date remain unannounced. Bezos said Amazon MGM ran a tight process with five finalists who underwent "real, old-fashioned screen tests," acting out three scenes in full costume on real sets; the final decision was made on Friday. Hollywood insiders have characterized Pattinson as a safe pick to draw audiences rather than betting on an unknown actor amid widespread industry cuts and consolidation. Matthew Belloni wrote that despite concerns he might be boring or represent passing up a chance at a new star, "with so much at stake for everyone involved, that all makes him the obvious pick." Other actors reported in frame during recent screen tests included Josh O'Connor, Callum Turner, and Jack Lowden. The BBC's Regan Morris contributed to this report.
items.title: Jeff Bezos on Robert Pattinson's Casting as James Bond

items.summary: Some of the world's most visited websites, including those of Zoom, HSBC, Equifax, CNN, Salesforce, and Ikea, were compromised in an effort to steal cryptocurrency and infect iPhones, according to security researcher Scott Helme on Monday. The malicious JavaScript was aimed at visitors to websites belonging to 178 organizations across multiple sectors through Optimizely, a website optimization platform. Optimizely confirmed the incident, stating it had identified 'a security incident in which an unauthorized party exploited a vulnerability in Experimentation and used it to add malicious JavaScript to some customer projects.' According to Helme, the scripts attempted to replace cryptocurrency payment addresses with the attacker's wallet. The malicious script also sought to capture payment card details as users entered them, steal cookies and screenshots, and deploy exploit code targeting Apple's iOS devices. Cybersecurity firm Hudson Rock said it had also found evidence that the affected sites had served malicious code to visitors. Apple said in an email the underlying vulnerabilities targeted by the hackers were fixed last year and users running up-to-date software would have been protected from exploitation. Optimizely said it had fixed the vulnerability, removed the injected code from affected projects, taken steps to secure affected user accounts and put additional protections in place to prevent unauthorized code from being delivered. Whether the malicious code had been successfully used in each case or the extent of any resulting compromises could not be immediately determined. Salesforce and Ikea said they were investigating the incident linked to Optimizely script changes; Salesforce disabled scripts from the platform as a precaution, while Equifax stopped using the platform after investigation found no evidence of compromise to its systems. Zoom disabled Optimizely across its production environments as a precautionary measure without identifying any impact on customer data yet, and HSBC said unauthorized scripts were not active on its websites. items.summary: Jensen Huang made an eleventh-hour appeal on social media for the Nvidia board to allow him to return as chief executive, writing that he would be 'honored' if directors decided his return served shareholders, employees, and America. The board has declined, maintaining its decision to remove him from leadership. Huang built Nvidia into a multi-trillion-dollar company at the center of the artificial intelligence revolution, but investors increasingly view his presence as adding risk to the valuation amid broader uncertainty in AI and tech. Speculation about an extra-marital affair with Alice Huang—an alleged Chinese spy—later expanded to include two other affairs involving Nvidia staff members. The FBI and US Justice Department are investigating how these relationships could raise national security concerns, particularly given that the US maintains export controls on Nvidia's chips originally designed for gaming but now used in AI applications. Because Huang was central to developing those chips, his liaisons create uncertainty about whether information has leaked to China, which would undermine investor confidence in Nvidia's technological edge. Nvidia's stock fell 33 per cent from its October peak over a month and is effectively in a bear market; the Blue Wave of US midterm elections served as a circuit-breaker for the valuation, with states like Texas resisting data centre expansion that threatens this key revenue stream. Hyperscalers rely on Nvidia chips to power their data centres, so investor insecurity about leadership compounded concerns about the company's ability to lead in computer chips. Despite strong support and hopes of reconsideration, board chair Harvey Jones declined to address Huang's resignation or ongoing investigation during a third-quarter earnings call while backing interim CEO Colette Kress—whom he described as talented with confidence in her 'integrity and ability to deliver.' Kress defended the team since Huang's departure. Analysts say executives are drawing firm lines to ring-fence the affairs' impact on valuation; Spaceship VP of investments Jason Sedawie noted the first call was steady and business-like, a shift from Jensen's usual approach, while Floodlines Research's Anna Wu said 'the reason hasn't changed: Huang is still tied to too much uncertainty and risk,' adding it tests whether markets believe in the rockstar or the numbers. Henry Jennings of Marcus Today characterized Huang as 'not the Messiah, just a very naughty boy' and warned that welcoming him back would harm governance credibility while keeping Jensen as a meme. Nvidia reported revenue up 20 per cent for the third quarter to $US115 billion ($170 billion), leaving open whether new leadership can sustain growth amid ongoing fallout from Huang's affairs; analysts remain uncertain about Nvidia's future under Colette Kress, who also serves as finance chief and is now interim CEO. Anna Wu noted that 'the board's credibility is at stake,' while Henry Jennings observed the board may have been premature in sacking Huang but acknowledged 'that ship has sailed.' The market appears to accept that Nvidia can operate without Huang, though his talents are now considered largely irrelevant given the emphasis on governance practices and established procedures. Kress stated 'We've got this' as she defended her team's work since Huang's departure.
