items.summary: On Monday (Nov 16), the US Department of Commerce announced tighter controls on exports of advanced artificial intelligence chips to Singapore, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia and Brazil, citing a 'higher-than-normal' risk that the chips could be illegally diverted to China. The restrictions take effect with companies needing a US licence by mid-February next year to continue serving Chinese-headquartered customers or face future export restrictions; US-headquartered firms are exempt as long as shipments are reported. Analysts say the rules create near-term uncertainty and reputational risk for Southeast Asia's AI ambitions, though they also present an opportunity for the region to strengthen its regulatory standing. Josh Gilbert of eToro called it 'a speed bump for Singapore's AI ambitions,' noting investors will want clarity moving forward. The restrictions follow the Nvidia-Megaspeed scandal, which added political pressure on Washington to restrict China's access to advanced computing capacity rented overseas; Megaspeed said Sunday that it conducted 'legitimate and lawful business.' Matthias Hendrichs, a Singapore-based advisor to AI companies, explained that over the last two years most reported cases of chips or computing power reaching Chinese companies passed through Southeast Asia. Under the new controls, non-American-owned regional cloud operators serving Chinese customers must obtain separate US licences at scale, while firms renting capacity from US providers will be less affected; he also flagged traders and system integrators who buy chips here and ship them on, plus telcos, research institutes and sovereign AI projects wanting to own their own chips. Hendrichs expects 'delays of months' for new projects and said the bigger near-term problem is uncertainty: 'If you can't tell a lender when the chips arrive, the financing waits,' citing data centre deals in Malaysia that were put on hold before the rule was introduced. Gilbert agreed that licences for Chinese clients 'won't come easily,' warning some investment plans could be held until companies see how strictly rules are applied. In the wider regional context, Dr Maria Monica Wihardja of ISEAS-Yusof Ishak Institute noted Southeast Asian governments have sought to remain neutral amid US-China rivalry and open to data centre investments from both sides; she described a 'dual-stack nature' in these countries that increases the perception they are also 'friends to their own friends' enemies.' Among the four Southeast Asian countries, Singapore and Malaysia have export control laws or strategic trade management frameworks, while Thailand has not fully implemented its framework. Indonesia has no dedicated regime, relying on 'scattered customs, import-export and sector-specific laws,' which Wihardja said weakens export links by allowing imported goods to be loosely re-exported without clear legal consequences. Complex data centre ownership structures spanning private equity firms, pension funds and major cloud providers also make it hard to establish who controls operations and is accountable for decisions. According to the UN Trade and Development's Global Investment Trends Monitor in January this year, Thailand and Malaysia were among the world's top recipients of data centre investment in the first three quarters of 2025, drawing US$9 billion and US$4 billion respectively. Hendrichs said companies can still access AI capabilities through US cloud providers so adoption continues; 'What takes a hit is the ambition to be the place where the computing sits,' he added, noting Malaysia could face greater exposure because it built the most capacity with some demand coming from China. Experts see a silver lining: restrictions could push countries to strengthen frameworks, including Indonesia introducing dedicated strategic trade management legislation and Thailand implementing its existing framework. Wihardja warned that failing to reform risks deepening reputational harm and hurting medium- to long-term growth as semiconductors, data centres and AI become new sources of growth; 'This is a good wake-up call and can make the region a more attractive destination for AI and data centre investment in the medium and long run.' For Singapore specifically, Hendrichs said the issue is less about trade volume than its standing as a trusted hub. The Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry and the Ministry of Digital Development and Information began talks with the US on Tuesday regarding trusted access for companies here.
items.title: US chip export curbs test Southeast Asia's AI ambitions while offering a chance to strengthen regulatory oversight

items.summary: The Australian Law Reform Commission (ALRC) has tabled 47 recommendations to reform the country’s surrogacy framework, aiming to make domestic surrogacy a viable and safer pathway to parenthood while aligning with international legal obligations. ALRC president Justice Mordy Bromberg argued that current laws fail both to enable responsible family formation through surrogacy and to protect against exploitation, instead driving Australians toward overseas arrangements where harm is most likely. The review found inconsistent laws and criminal sanctions push parents underground and abroad, increasing rather than reducing risk. While the exact number of domestic gestational births remains hard to determine, estimates suggest they more than tripled from 27 births in 2014 to 84 births in 2023. Overseas surrogacy also rose substantially over a similar period, from 246 in 2015 to 375 births in 2024 — an increase of more than 40% — occurring as the overall birthrate has fallen. The report recommends retaining the ban on commercial surrogacy while granting surrogates greater compensation covering medical costs, loss of earnings including superannuation, and other pregnancy-related expenses. ALRC principal legal officer Jacinth Pathmanathan said the framework would also require intended parents to register, receive official guidance, obtain legal advice in both Australia and the overseas country, and take reasonable steps to avoid unlawful or high-risk arrangements; failing these obligations could result in a civil penalty. The report is now with the commonwealth attorney general for consideration.
items.title: Australia’s surrogacy laws could be reformed under proposed changes

items.summary: With Alaska's final Senate race called two weeks after the midterms, Democrat Mary Peltola defeated Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan to become Alaska's next senator. This victory makes her the first Democrat elected to the state's Senate since 2008 and gives Democrats control of all 56 seats in the chamber. The party gained nine Senate seats overall in the midterms, positioning them decisively back in the majority beginning next year when they are expected to pursue aggressive lawmaking and investigations. Peltola, a former US House lawmaker who grew up along Alaska's Kuskokwim River and became the first Alaska native elected to Congress after winning a 2022 special election following Don Young's death, previously lost her own re-election to Republican Nick Begich in 2024 before entering this race. Her campaign faced controversy when the New York Times reported that her staffers were involved in recruiting another Republican challenger named Dan Sullivan onto the ballot; while Peltola denied involvement and state officials initially sought his removal, Alaska's supreme court ruled in June that he be allowed on the ballot. Trump called for Peltola's prosecution over the alleged scheme, prompting criminal and civil inquiries from federal prosecutors as well as a separate investigation by the state governor. Alaskans' frustration with rising costs drove much of her appeal: as the largest US state reliant on oil prices affected by Trump's tariffs and his decision to attack Iran earlier this year, gas prices in some interior communities jumped into double-digits per gallon while diesel price increases raised costs for groceries and alcohol due to sea shipments. Peltola adopted the slogan 'fish, family, freedom' and positioned herself as an advocate for expanding oil production and addressing bycatch linked to declining salmon runs. As a Yup'ik woman, she will join Minnesota senator-elect Peggy Flanagan of the White Earth band of Ojibwe as the first two Native American women in the US Senate; Peltola posted a 1995 photograph showing her wearing a Miss National Congress of American Indians winner's sash. Sullivan remained aligned with Trump even as his popularity declined, particularly in Alaska according to some surveys, and did not join other vulnerable Republicans urging an end to the war with Iran while accusing Peltola of disrespecting voters after reports that she used a homophobic slur and abused her staff.
items.title: Mary Peltola Defeats Dan Sullivan; Democrats Secure 56 Senate Seats

items.summary: Chinese President Xi Jinping opened the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) meeting on Wednesday in Shenzhen, calling for stronger international cooperation on artificial intelligence and free trade ahead of an expected Thursday meeting with US President Donald Trump. Addressing growing pressure to manage AI's risks, Xi urged leaders to "actively build partnerships for scientific and technological innovation, deepen cooperation in the digital economy and artificial intelligence and promote a green and low-carbon transition." He argued that converting China's innovation strengths into growth momentum could provide economic impetus across Asia-Pacific while fostering shared regional prosperity. On trade, Xi called for eliminating barriers and promoting inclusive development, stating China would "provide a more stable, predictable and beneficial environment for global enterprises" by expanding access in manufacturing and services through deep-seated reform that begins with lowering tariffs and exploring new regulations and management standards. The remarks arrive as tensions between the two largest economies intensify: Trump has imposed wide-ranging tariffs met by Chinese counter-levies and threats to withhold key exports, a truce reached at last year's South Korea summit is set to expire in January, and the US this week announced tougher restrictions on exporting advanced semiconductors used to train and run AI models. The new controls target chip smuggling as well as grey-market rentals of Nvidia-designed computing power from data centres abroad; Nvidia reported strong earnings Wednesday but its results were overshadowed by a scandal involving former CEO Jensen Huang's affair with a woman suspected of spying for China, which US officials say is relevant to national security concerns underlying the export restrictions. Xi and Trump are expected to discuss world peace at the summit, according to Chinese statements. The article notes these developments unfold amid ongoing trade friction but does not detail specific figures or outcomes from any negotiations between the two leaders. France 24 reported this item with AFP. France 24 reported this item with AFP.
items.title: Xi Jinping calls for global AI and free-trade cooperation at APEC summit in Shenzhen

items.summary: As Victoria's election day approaches, opinion polling shows support for the Labor state government has turned 'from bad to diabolical.' Earlier in June and July, Labor, the Liberals, and One Nation were all polling first preferences in the mid-20s, suggesting a complex result with One Nation near a tipping point that could sweep many seats. Combined with Greens competitiveness in inner Melbourne, this scenario would have seen the government defend its seats against three parties across the state's 88 districts. The then-premier Jacinta Allan was replaced at that point, but the slide away from Labor did not halt. Several pollsters recorded strengthening Coalition support in recent weeks as both Labor and One Nation slid. Polls collected in November put statewide Coalition support just above 30 per cent, with the gap between the Coalition and One Nation widening since June and July to nearly 10 percentage points on average. This is important because the Coalition's path to majority government becomes very difficult if it falls into third place in many electorates; while it benefits from preferences from both Labor and One Nation voters, it needs to stay first or second to receive them. Polls suggest this will happen in far fewer seats than mid-year, which also drops the likelihood of One Nation winning a huge number of seats and depriving Liberal leader Jess Wilson of a majority. This takes the sting out of Ben Carroll's warnings about a Coalition government allied with Pauline Hanson's party, and even raises questions about whether the premier's negative campaigning has backfired by sending more soft voters toward the Liberals. A Resolve poll for Nine newspapers this month found more voters were comfortable with the idea of the Coalition governing with One Nation than uncomfortable; conversely, voters felt much less comfortable about Labor governing with the Greens. While the situation appears markedly improved for Jess Wilson, Labor is facing not just defeat but an absolute wipe-out. There is a real prospect of the government coming third on primaries statewide, while two-party-preferred results over recent weeks have consistently estimated the Coalition at 55 or 56 per cent and Labor at 45 or 46 per cent. These blunt numbers equate to a swing of roughly ten percentage points since the 2022 election; a uniform swing that large would see the Coalition win around 30 seats from Labor, which is well above the 16 gains needed for a majority and gives the opposition substantial breathing room toward what could be a Labor rout. The article notes this is not expected to be a uniform swing, so some of those seats may be held or lost to One Nation instead — especially in Melbourne's outer fringe seats including Sunbury and Bass, and rural seats like Eureka and Ripon. Where Labor once hoped One Nation would be a thorn in the Coalition's side by taking regional seats, it now appears to be a bigger threat to the government itself: Labor and Green voters in regional Victoria are more likely to preference the Coalition over One Nation, so One Nation probably needs to beat the Nationals on primaries to stay ahead after preferences. Liberal voters will most likely preference One Nation above Labor, as suggested by the opposition's how-to-vote card, which makes it easier for One Nation to win Melbourne seats from Labor if it can beat the Liberal candidate and poll within spitting distance of Labor — a scenario that could send chills up the spine of Labor MPs nationally and prove Pauline Hanson is a threat to both sides. Even if One Nation does not win many seats, polling suggests records will be broken: Labor could record the worst primary vote of any sitting government in Australia since at least World War II, while the Coalition might reach majority from a record low vote. Aside from the ACT's first election under self-determination with its unique circumstances, the combined Labor-Coalition vote never dipped below 65 per cent in any Australian election between 1945 and 2025; it fell to 56.5 per cent in South Australia in March when One Nation recorded its best ever statewide vote — a low watermark Victorian voters may now hand down the major parties.
items.title: Victorian Labor polling turns from bad to diabolical as Coalition edges toward majority

items.summary: Lt Col Brandon Carroll Tyner, a 41-year-old US Army officer who has served since 2008 and previously deployed to Afghanistan and Iraq, was arrested near Gloucester last week by British counter-terror police. At the time of his arrest he was based at Imjin Barracks in Innsworth, Gloucestershire, which serves as the headquarters of Nato's Allied Rapid Reaction Corps. He is now held in US military custody over suspected national security and espionage allegations. Tyner was arrested under section one and section three of the National Security Act 2023, relating to obtaining or disclosing protected information and assisting a foreign intelligence service. British police had initially said he was being held in London after his arrest on 10 November. The day after that arrest, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters in Moscow that Russia was 'unaware' of what the matter concerned and stated it had nothing to do with it. Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, head of Counter Terrorism Policing, said a decision was made to pass the investigation to US partners so they could progress it, describing the allegations as extremely serious and saying the collective response should send a strong message that such espionage activity will be met swiftly and robustly. The arrest resulted from a long-running MI5 operation in collaboration with the FBI. Tyner had been entrusted with sensitive information at his NATO posting which would have been damaging if leaked to Russia, though he was not confirmed as spying for Russia specifically. Detectives sent the Crown Prosecution Service a file on the alleged spying, but the Attorney General's Office and US authorities became involved before it emerged that Lieutenant Colonel Tyner would be taken into custody by the US military rather than standing trial in the UK under the National Security Act 2023; he will instead face proceedings under the US Uniform Code of Military Justice. FBI director Kash Patel said an army officer was placed in custody as a result of an espionage investigation and close cooperation between the bureau, the US Army, and various UK partners, adding that the FBI has zero tolerance for anyone who betrays their oath to the United States or puts national security at risk. US Brig Gen Sean Stinchon described the case as a stark warning to any service member suspected of violating their oath, saying whenever someone is suspected of betraying trust and jeopardising collective defence, they will be identified and justice served. The report does not establish whether Tyner was spying for Russia specifically or confirm details beyond the espionage suspicions raised by British authorities; it also notes that his arrest followed a long-running operation rather than detailing its full scope.
items.title: US Army officer arrested in UK on spying suspicion taken into US military custody

items.summary: Ahead of the 33rd APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting, China Media Group (CMG) hosted an event titled "Asia-Pacific of One Heart: Creating the Future Together – A CMG Media Gathering" in Shenzhen, Guangdong Province, on Monday, November 16, 2026. The gathering convened 69 representatives from media organizations across 62 countries, alongside delegates from Chinese media, businesses, and cultural and artistic sectors for discussions on technological innovation and media cooperation. Qi Zhuquan, vice president of CMG, addressed the event, calling on Asia-Pacific media to promote openness and cooperation, document innovation and development, foster mutual learning among civilizations, strengthen public understanding of a shared future, and contribute to common prosperity. Chen Xiaowei, deputy head of the Publicity Department of the CPC Guangdong Provincial Committee and director of the Information Office of the Guangdong Provincial People's Government, noted that APEC economies account for about two-thirds of Guangdong's foreign trade and more than 80% of its foreign investment, underscoring the province's close economic ties with the region; he added that people-to-people exchanges are as important as trade links and invited media representatives to experience Guangdong's openness. Alonso Millán Zepeda, director general of Mexican public cultural television station Canal 22, spoke of longstanding Mexico-China friendship and his organization's cooperation with CMG, calling for closer collaboration in cultural content production, audiovisual program exchanges, and exchanges among young media professionals. Presentations were also given by John Liu, executive editor at Bloomberg LP; Andrey Popov, a correspondent with TASS in Shanghai; Dong Mingzhu, chairwoman of Gree Electric Appliances, who highlighted the company's experience in manufacturing, research and development, core technology breakthroughs, innovation, talent, and health; Dr. Hua Wenli, a scientific officer with the China Meteorological Administration's World Meteorological Centre Beijing office, who introduced MAZU, China's intelligent meteorological early-warning solution and its use across multiple countries to improve disaster preparedness and international cooperation; and hosts Liu Yue, CMG host Liu Xin, and China-Arab TV reporter Fang Haoming. The event featured cultural performances drawing on diverse international influences. A special program featuring the event is scheduled for release on November 17 on CMG's new media platforms, including CCTV News, CGTN, and Voice of the Greater Bay Area.
items.title: CMG Media Gathering Brings Asia-Pacific Voices Together in Shenzhen

items.summary: The 33rd APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting is themed 'Building an Asia-Pacific Community to Prosper Together,' and the region it represents accounts for more than 60% of global economic output. Rhys Roberts, president of the Australia-China Business Council (ACBC), discusses China's importance as a trading partner for both Australia and the wider Asia-Pacific region. He notes that China remains key to trade across the area. The article highlights several sectors where China and Australia are exploring new areas of cooperation with significant growth potential: iron ore, premium agricultural products, green technology, electric vehicles, and batteries. These represent emerging opportunities beyond traditional trade flows. This interview frames China's market as central to business prospects for companies operating throughout the Asia-Pacific region during this APEC gathering in 2025. The piece is presented through an ACBC lens, emphasizing bilateral Australia-China commercial ties rather than offering a broader critical assessment of regional dynamics or trade dependencies beyond what Roberts asserts about cooperation potential and China's standing as a key partner. No specific figures on volumes, values, or growth rates are provided in the source material; only the more-than-60% global economic output figure for the Asia-Pacific region is stated explicitly, along with the sector names identified as areas of prospective collaboration.
items.title: ACBC President: China Remains Key to Asia-Pacific Trade

items.summary: Shenzhen is hosting the 33rd APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting on November 18 and 19, 2026, under the theme "Building an Asia-Pacific Community to Prosper Together." The forum's member economies differ greatly in size, history, political system and stage of development. Around 3 billion people live across these members, which have produced over 60% of world GDP and nearly 50% of world trade. A recurring framing for this diversity is the "big family" metaphor: Chinese President Xi Jinping first invoked it at his 2013 APEC debut in Bali, Indonesia, saying China cannot develop in isolation while the Asia-Pacific cannot prosper without China, and repeated it in a written speech to the APEC CEO Summit in 2023. The article argues that this diversity is why APEC does not operate like most international bodies: by its own account it runs on voluntary cooperation and consensus, carries no binding force, gives every member's views equal weight, and respects each member's right to development. Xi described these principles as "the APEC Approach," built on voluntarism, consensus-building and incremental progress, adding that forcing uniformity will not advance regional cooperation. The record cited for this model is that over the past three decades the Asia-Pacific lowered its average tariff rate from 17% to 5% and generated 70% of global economic growth, outcomes attributed to dialogue, coordination and measures each economy chose at a pace it could sustain rather than dictates from powerful members. The article notes economists find this logic familiar: flexible arrangements reduce participation costs for weaker members, let them advance as capacity expands, and prevent one dispute from halting everything else; voluntary progress may look slow but consensus tends to endure so modest steps accumulate. Seeking common ground while shelving differences is described not as evasion but as a way of working, with the shared goal being growth, better lives and more resilient economies, while real differences rooted in history, institutions and development levels are acknowledged. The approach is presented as especially important amid rising protectionism, strained supply chains, and new opportunities and disputes from artificial intelligence and the green transition; Xi's 2023 statement that "development is only possible with cooperation; absence of cooperation is the biggest risk" is cited in this context. Shared prosperity is also framed by who benefits rather than merely how fast the region grows: if digital gains accrue to a few large platforms while developing members lack infrastructure and skills, the family loses its warmth, so capacity building and narrowing development gaps deserve as much weight as frontier issues. China's role as host is characterized not as making decisions but as setting the table; Xi said at last year's APEC handover session in Gyeongju, South Korea that he looked forward to all parties gathering in Shenzhen to jointly discuss regional development plans. Shenzhen itself is cited as an illustration of openness having transformed a small fishing village into a modern international metropolis within decades. The article concludes that the "big family" is more than a figure of speech: respect for differences broadens consensus, voluntary cooperation makes it last, and common ground turns diversity into complementary strengths, with the region needing many voices singing in harmony rather than one voice drowning out the rest.
items.title: APEC 2026: Shenzhen hosts a diverse Asia-Pacific under voluntary cooperation

items.summary: A senior US defence official has publicly criticised Ukraine's 'deep strike' campaign against Russia, arguing that the long-range attacks have failed to end the war and may have strengthened Moscow's position. Under Secretary of Defence Elbridge Colby, speaking from NATO headquarters in Brussels on Tuesday, stated: "Our assessment is that such strikes have not been effective in driving an end to the war, nor do they contribute to blunting Russia's advances on the front line." He added that these strikes—particularly those targeting civilian infrastructure such as Wildberries—have likely hardened both the Russian public's resolve and the Kremlin's willingness to escalate. Colby said future US support should instead focus on "enabling and advancing Ukraine's ability to hold the line of battle and where possible make gains." The comments drew sharp pushback from European officials. German Defence Minister Boris Pistorius dismissed the warning as "quite a stupid thing," while British counterpart Wes Streeting asserted there was "no doubt" that Ukraine's long-range strikes had helped degrade Putin's war machine, buying time and saving lives. Colby noted that Ukrainian forces have increasingly targeted energy infrastructure such as oil refineries and terminals, along with military sites like air bases, to hamper the Russian economy. This follows earlier demands from US President Donald Trump for Ukraine to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries over concerns about rising diesel fuel prices. The dispute coincided with Zelensky's renewed appeals at a meeting of the Ukraine Defence Contact Group in Brussels via video link, where he urged allies to speed up deliveries of Patriot and IRIS-T interceptor missiles from existing stocks and requested 40 additional F-16 fighter jets to bolster air defences. These pleas come as Ukraine prepares for another winter under heavy Russian bombardment, with Moscow repeatedly intensifying attacks on the country's energy sector during wartime winters in an attempt to break its resolve.
items.title: US official criticises Ukraine's deep strikes; European allies push back

items.summary: A court in The Hague on Tuesday convicted former Kosovo President Hashim Thaci of obstructing justice and attempting to influence witnesses during his war crimes trial, sentencing him to 17 months in prison. This term will be added to his existing 25-year sentence for war crimes handed down by the same court, the Kosovo Specialist Chambers, on September 16. According to the indictment of the Specialist Prosecutor's Office, Thaci had provided visitors at the detention facility with confidential information about witnesses and instructed them on how to influence their testimony. Three other men were also convicted: former head of the Kosovo Intelligence Agency Bashkim Smakaj, former Minister of Justice Hajredin Kuci, and Fadil Fazliu. Thaci was the former political leader of the Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA) during the 1998-1999 Kosovo War and is viewed by many in his home country as a hero; his September war crimes conviction was greeted with anger and dismay. He has vowed to appeal both convictions, which touch on deep sensitivities regarding the role of former KLA leaders and trust in judicial institutions. The government responded swiftly, issuing a statement asserting that justice must be fair, transparent, and credible, built not only on decisions but also on how they are reached. The Kosovo Specialist Chambers was established in 2015 by the parliament of Kosovo at the instigation of the European Union and the United States to investigate serious crimes allegedly committed by KLA members during and after the war; for security reasons including witness intimidation concerns, it is located in The Hague in the Netherlands. After the September first-instance convictions, state authorities established a working group chaired by Foreign Minister Glauk Konjufca, which includes parliament members, to draft an appeal strategy. Prime Minister Albin Kurti stated that the government believes the first-instance judgment was unjust both legally and morally and is working to secure a correction at the appeals level. Separately, Kosovo's parliament is considering amendments expected to be adopted that would narrow the court's mandate by limiting its jurisdiction time period, capping maximum prison sentences at 15 years, allowing sentences to be served in Kosovo, and introducing presidential pardons for persons convicted by final decisions. Political analyst Artan Muhaxheri warned this initiative could appear as an attempt to interfere with the judicial process before a final verdict is reached, stressing that it must not conflict with Kosovo's international obligations toward the European Union. Ehat Miftaraj of the Kosovo Law Institute (IKD) noted that although the chambers were established by Kosovo itself, the process has created an impression that judges and prosecutors treated both accused and Kosovo with distrust and a condescending approach; he emphasized that criticism is legitimate but there remains room for criticism of both sides between lawful critique and attempts to delegitimize courts. items.summary: Nvidia Corp. announced it is no longer shipping licensed Hopper data center chips to China, even though the company had won US government approval last year to sell a version of that model to the Asian nation. Interim CEO Colette Kress told analysts during an earnings call on Tuesday that Nvidia sold $2.4 billion worth of these licensed Hopper products in the third quarter. She added that future guidance includes no licensed Hopper data center products and confirmed shipments have ended, though she did not explain why they were stopping. The shift represents a notable change for a company that had long advocated greater access to Chinese customers; Jensen Huang, who was ousted as CEO last week amid reports of multiple extramarital affairs, had been the most vocal proponent of exports to China. Huang disclosed an affair with a woman now under US government investigation for potentially aiding China's spy agency and possibly helping smuggle chips into the country, though Beijing denied attempting to spy on him. On Monday, the Trump administration moved to apply greater scrutiny to processor exports to several countries and limit chip sales abroad when data center buyers plan to grant Chinese companies remote access to advanced AI chips and servers. Nvidia had earlier pushed for permission to sell more advanced Blackwell chips to China; that request was never granted, but President Donald Trump approved the sale of Hopper processors known as H200s, which are two generations behind Nvidia's leading Rubin family of chips, reflecting the strong personal relationship Huang built with Trump. Harvey Jones, appointed Nvidia's first chair last week, said the board recognizes it is "living in a world" where national security dynamics are reshaping its marketplace and that the next CEO must navigate those conditions carefully. Nvidia also announced Tuesday that it would form a board committee focused on national security and export controls. The article notes these developments were reported by Bloomberg as of November 18, 2026, without further elaboration from Kress on the reasons behind the halted shipments or additional details on the administration's new scrutiny measures beyond what was stated Monday.
items.title: Nvidia Halts Licensed Hopper Chip Shipments to China Despite Prior US Approval

items.summary: The Mukesh Ambani-led Reliance Group is exploring manufacturing partnerships for a planned low-earth orbit broadband constellation of roughly 1,600 satellites (quantity-108-113), which people familiar with the matter describe as an Indian-controlled alternative to Elon Musk's Starlink. The network would support newly-listed Jio Platforms Ltd., and Reliance is in talks with Indian satellite manufacturers, technology startups, and larger industrial groups while offering to fund required infrastructure; sources asked not to be identified because plans remain private (entity-30-44). India currently produces fewer than 15 satellites a year (quantity-845-858), whereas the proposed constellation would require output of about 200 satellites annually, placing Reliance at the center of efforts to close that gap (quantity-957-971). The approach mirrors New Delhi's push to use private-sector investment for strategic capabilities, exemplified by Tata Group investments in semiconductor and electronics manufacturing under government-backed initiatives. Reliance plans to combine domestic manufacturing with imports, including at least 400 satellites from the US (quantity-1344-1358), while pursuing a September 2027 test mission and wider deployment beginning early 2028; completion is now targeted for 2035, later than an earlier goal of 2030 due to manufacturing and launch constraints. The company is discussing procurement with two US firms and evaluating European suppliers but is not considering China as a source (place-1792-1797). Although the constellation could compete with Starlink's more than 10,000-satellite global network, Reliance's system would be geared primarily toward India's connectivity and strategic requirements. Strengthening domestic space capabilities has become key for New Delhi following a recent border conflict with Pakistan (place-2503-2511), prompting increased investment in surveillance satellites and private partnerships. Industry executives say launch capacity may prove the bigger challenge than manufacturing, which can be expanded with sufficient investment; deploying thousands of satellites would require significantly greater launch frequency and access to suitable orbital slots. Amal Chandran, CEO of satellite manufacturer HEX20 (entity-3158-3171), stated: "Manufacturing at scale is doable but the real challenge will be to ensure there are enough rocket launches happening in India for the satellites to be placed in the desired orbit." Starlink's entry into India remains subject to regulatory and security scrutiny, with concerns over oversight of foreign networks during geopolitical tension strengthening the case for domestically controlled alternatives. An email seeking Reliance comments elicited no response (entity-462-470). The item was published on November 18, 2026 (date-3554-3571).
items.title: Reliance Pursues 1,600-Satellite Constellation to Counter Starlink in India

items.summary: Nvidia is under fresh regulatory examination as a civil investigation into the company unfolds. This probe compounds an unprecedented crisis for the AI chipmaker following the recent resignation of CEO Jensen Huang, whose departure followed revelations of multiple extramarital affairs—one with a woman suspected by US officials of being a Chinese intelligence asset and another involving a company employee. Beijing denied attempting to spy on Huang per Reuters reporting, while Nvidia's board announced on November 8 that it launched an investigation after reports he was targeted by a foreign intelligence effort. Questions persist about Huang's continued influence; under company filings he retains the right to nominate two directors ahead of the annual shareholder meeting, provided nominees meet independence requirements. Despite leadership uncertainty, business outlook remains intact: Nvidia reported third-quarter earnings and revenue growth driven by AI chip demand, forecasting fourth-quarter revenue of $126 billion to $134 billion for fiscal 2027.
items.title: Nvidia faces regulatory scrutiny amid leadership crisis

items.summary:
After resigning as CEO of Nvidia last week amid revelations about extramarital affairs, Jensen Huang remains a significant influence over the chipmaker through his shareholder voting power. Chip industry executives, investors and customers are closely examining what role he will play going forward, with director nomination rights emerging as a potential lever to shape the company's future leadership.

Under Nvidia's governance rules, any shareholder or group owning more than 3% of voting power for at least three years is entitled to nominate directors who appear in proxy materials and vote at the annual meeting, typically held in June. Data from LSEG indicates that Huang and entities tied to him have owned more than 3% of Nvidia's shares for over three years; he currently holds roughly 3.5% of the company.

The board initiated an investigation on November 8 following reporting that Huang had been targeted by a foreign intelligence effort, though Reuters could not determine whether his conduct violated the company's bylaws or charter. Neither Nvidia nor a representative for Huang responded to requests for comment.

Huang resigned in the wake of reports about his extramarital affairs. Since then, figures including Elon Musk, employees, investors and US President Donald Trump have advocated for his return as CEO. However, three people with knowledge of the matter told Reuters that the board was not considering reinstating him at the time. Huang released a statement on Tuesday saying he "would be honored" to return if the board decided it served shareholders' and employees' best interests.

On Tuesday after market close, Nvidia forecast quarterly revenue above Wall Street estimates, providing some relief to investors amid uncertainty surrounding Huang's departure.
items.title: Jensen Huang's board nomination rights may outweigh his resignation from Nvidia

items.summary: According to people briefed on the matter who asked not to be identified because the details are not public, Anthropic — the maker of the Claude chatbot along with its seven co-founders — is marketing 825 million shares for $70 to $78 each in filings with the US Securities and Exchange Commission. At that price point, including a separate $26 billion private placement, the IPO would raise about $90.4 billion. Banks are expected to stop taking orders at 4 p.m. on Tuesday in New York, per these sources. If Anthropic prices at the top of its range, it would carry a fully diluted valuation of roughly $1.4 trillion. The people involved noted that deliberations were ongoing and offering details could still change; an Anthropic representative did not immediately comment. At the stated price, the deal would exceed SpaceX's $75 billion base offering as the largest listing ever, though Anthropic's potential valuation might fall below Elon Musk's company at its debut of $1.77 trillion market value. To bolster investor interest ahead of pricing, Anthropic has held events such as a Friday livestreamed discussion between CEO Dario Amodei and JPMorgan Chase & Co. CEO Jamie Dimon. The reported figures are attributed to unnamed sources rather than confirmed by the company or public filings.
items.title: Anthropic IPO priced at $70–$78 would raise ~$90.4 billion and imply a ~$1.4 trillion valuation

items.summary: On November 18 in Washington, an Apple update failure added to a series of major technology outages across the United States. Apple acknowledged on its system status page that full outages affected Apple Music, App Store and AppleCare services, with iCloud sign-in also experiencing issues; Downdetector reported a spike in complaints about Apple Pay as well. In a statement emailed to reporters, Apple said many systems were back up after an internal update caused the outage and it was working to bring remaining systems online. Marriott International, the largest US hotel operator with 10,200 properties and more than 1.8 million rooms under its corporate umbrella, also reported technology issues affecting reservations and check-ins, according to users on Reddit; Downdetector likewise reported a Marriott outage, though the company had not responded to an AP inquiry. The Apple and Marriott problems followed other breakdowns in recent days: United Airlines suffered an outage lasting more than 90 minutes that delayed departing flights, coming just after a Federal Aviation Administration network malfunction prompted a nationwide ground stop that delayed hundreds of flights and stranded hundreds of thousands of travelers; several major US banks and the money transfer service Zelle saw customers struggle to access online accounts after a technical issue at JPMorgan Chase rippled through the financial system. United said there was no indication its outage was cybersecurity related, while Chase confirmed Monday the problems were not caused by a cyberattack and that systems had returned to normal as of Tuesday. Earlier in the week, a global Microsoft outage disrupted email and workplace tools worldwide, interrupting Microsoft 365 services including Outlook, Teams and AI assistant Copilot; Microsoft stated there was no indication the disruptions stemmed from malicious activity or artificial intelligence agents. Collectively, these events underscore how heavily daily life now depends on sprawling technological networks and the risks inherent in their massive scope (AP). items.summary: Microsoft Chairman and CEO Satya Nadella explained the rationale behind the company's voluntary exit offer in a podcast interview with The Pragmatic Engineer. He said the initiative is designed to give employees greater flexibility over their career choices as work, job opportunities, and organizational structures change. Nadella acknowledged that opportunities within Microsoft would take a different shape in coming years, requiring changes to team sizes, workflows, and how employees are organized across the company. He emphasized creating new internal opportunities so workers can acquire skills valuable both inside Microsoft and in the wider market, whether they work on Windows or AI training. The transformation also requires reconsidering workforce organization overall; Nadella said "the 200,000 people at Microsoft and growing will have to be configured in different ways." He framed the voluntary program as giving employees more agency over their long-term economic opportunities. His own career path from individual contributor to top leadership shaped his view of employee growth. The comments accompany a Voluntary Exit Offer (VEO) extended to approximately 60,000 eligible employees across four countries: India, the United States, the United Kingdom, and Canada. Nadella acknowledged this period involves significant change and said he could not assume work would remain unchanged, adding that Microsoft wanted to be transparent while creating new internal opportunities and supporting professional growth.
items.title: Nadella Explains Microsoft's Voluntary Exit Offer to ~60,000 Employees

items.summary: Nvidia reported a third quarter ended October 25, 2026 in which revenue reached $115.8 billion, a 103% increase from the year-ago period and a 20% rise over the previous quarter. In his first public comments since the scandal, Huang acknowledged personal mistakes and expressed willingness to return as chief executive if the board chose reinstatement; chairman Harvey Jones stated at the earnings call that the Board had unanimously accepted his resignation and did not intend to bring him back.

At the ET Wealth Expo 2026, during a panel titled 'Emerging arsenals of India's rich: Will these work in future', Rajesh Saluja argued that wealth-creation approaches are shifting toward preserving capital while ensuring long-term compounding. He noted earlier generations focused on maximising returns through businesses and traditional assets such as real estate and gold, whereas the next generation has greater access to financial markets, investment information and a wider range of products. Saluja said 'The biggest gift a generation can give to the next generation is to really create what is called an investment framework,' which he proposed should rest on three buckets: a safety pot, a compounding pot and an opportunistic pot. Allocation across these buckets, he said, depends on experience, risk appetite, horizon and liquidity needs.

Saluja observed that illiquid alternative investments should not automatically be treated as risky; the greater danger is being forced to sell at the wrong time. He indicated that for high-net-worth and ultra-high-net-worth families around 15-30% of portfolios typically goes into liquid assets including high-quality fixed income, another 30-50% into compounding assets largely equities and equity-linked investments, and approximately 15-20% may go into alternatives. He also said alternatives are increasingly finding space within both fixed-income and equity allocations: about 15% to 20% in alternate fixed income such as private credit, performing credit and real estate funds, while 10-15% of equity could go into alternative growth investments like pre-IPO funds, private equity and venture capital.

Despite the popularity of alternatives, Saluja cautioned against chasing fashionable products. He said listed equities remain an established route for long-term wealth creation backed by a longer track record and compounding benefits, so investors should build a core portfolio of quality equities before diversifying into alternatives. He stressed that alternatives must justify their illiquidity with superior returns: 'For alternate 10-year products, we are talking about 18% to 22% compounded return. And out of the 200 funds available today in India, only 5% to 10% of them have been able to beat equity.' He warned against locking money into long-duration products without assessing fund-manager track records and urged investors to increase exposure gradually as they gain experience.

Saluja linked the expansion of India's wealth management industry to economic growth, rising wealth creation and increasing financialisation of household assets. He pointed to growing real-estate monetisation and a next-generation preference for simpler portfolios. Citing figures from the discussion, he said India has identified around 40,000 ultra-HNI families with portfolios of Rs 50-75 crore, while HNI families with roughly Rs 10 crore are estimated at approximately six lakh. He compared this to mature markets such as the US and concluded 'We are just at the tip of the iceberg. I think it has got a long-long runway.'

On behaviour, Saluja said temperament rather than intelligence determines outcomes, identifying three mistakes: investing in products one does not understand, chasing returns by overallocating to fashionable classes, and frequently entering and exiting markets. He emphasised discipline through cycles over trying to predict movements, saying 'Today, also the markets reward you for more staying and patience rather than brilliance and intelligence.' Illustrating this, he cited Rs 10 crore invested in a passive Nifty investment in 2005 growing to approximately Rs 144 crore over 21 years. He noted that an investment delivering 14% annualised returns over the same period could have generated significantly lower results if missed even some of its strongest days, and urged comparing products on post-tax and post-fee returns rather than headline figures.

Saluja also cautioned against assuming fixed income is inherently safer than equities, saying investors underestimate the research needed to evaluate credit and fixed-income products and should consider professional managers. Ultimately he said successful wealth management requires asset-allocation discipline, risk understanding, patience and a clear framework passed across generations.
items.title: Rajesh Saluja: India's wealthy should prioritise capital preservation as alternatives gain traction

The Cambridge Dictionary has named 'human' as its Word of the Year for 2026, defining it as "having the qualities, faults, and feelings that people have, as opposed to gods, animals, or machines." The dictionary explained that throughout history the adjective human signified people in contrast to animals and gods—and more recently machines—but increasingly appears in compounds such as 'human-written,' 'human-generated,' and 'human-made.' It now denotes something created by or typical of people rather than AI. Cambridge suggested this shift may be a natural linguistic development reflecting the ubiquity of AI, but could also signal "a turning point in our attitude towards artificial intelligence." The dictionary described 2026 as having been "defined by global debates on what it means to be human when AI is blurring the boundaries between people and machines."

Colin McIntosh, chief editor of Cambridge Dictionary, said that although AI had been a growing presence for years, in 2026 it seemed 'everywhere.' He noted this led to "a re-evaluation of what it means to be human, as a counterbalance to AI," pointing to "a newfound appreciation of the human factor in what we consume (with a consequent human premium)," and a new value placed on the human element. Cambridge said these observations were confirmed by its analysis of language data, internet trends, and search habits.

The article noted that 2026 saw rapid AI advancements across industries, with businesses and consumers increasingly valuing human creativity, craftsmanship, and authenticity as AI-generated content became common. The terms 'human-made' and the trend of a 'human premium' were cited as reflecting this shift toward recognizing human involvement in products and experiences.

Cambridge also referenced public interventions by intellectuals such as Geoffrey Hinton, an AI pioneer and Nobel laureate, who said: "We're creating alien beings. I'm willing to be selfish and choose humans." The dictionary listed four other shortlisted words alongside 'human': 'analogue' (relating to activities or devices that do not use the internet or digital technology), 'agent' (an AI system operating without human control, generally for making decisions rather than creating content), 'wholesome' (good for you and likely to improve your life physically, morally, or emotionally), and 'chic' (stylish and fashionable).

The article provided supporting context on AI capabilities: in May 2026, the University of California, San Diego published a study revealing empirical evidence that artificial intelligence systems passed the Turing Test. In 73% of cases, after a 15-minute text conversation, ChatGPT-4.5 was judged to be "human." The article further noted AI can now produce writing, art, and music passing as human-made content, with some questioning whether AI has achieved sentience.

The piece is authored by Swati Gandhi, a digital journalist specializing in international and geopolitical issues, who previously worked at Business Standard covering national affairs, politics, and business, and currently works at Live Mint. She holds a Bachelor's degree in English (Honours) from the University of Delhi and a Master's degree in Journalism and Mass Communication from Guru Gobind Singh Indraprastha University.

The article frames 2026 as potentially "a pivotal moment in the story of human versus machine" when viewed retrospectively.
items.title: Cambridge Dictionary Names 'Human' Its Word of the Year 2026 Amid AI Debate

items.summary: The article traces India's post-independence development drive, which by the late 1940s framed colonial rule itself as an obstacle to progress and then pursued that nationalist ambition so aggressively over roughly two decades that it materially improved daily life for only a few sections of society: the upper and middle classes. The Films Division documentary I am 20 from 1967 captures this elite experience, with interviewed youth expressing sentiments such as 'I would say I am better off than my father was in almost every respect'; 'Well, I think I need 50 sarees'; and 'Of course [my needs] are more. I have more money to buy things...I see more things in the market, so I buy them.' By the 1970s such scepticism entered mainstream public discourse, though it had long been an everyday reality for subaltern communities. In the mid-1970s the Indian Council of Social Sciences Research (ICSSR) launched a research project titled 'Alternatives in Development,' and scholar Rajni Kothari published a two-part article series under that title in its 1979 newsletter to expound the philosophy behind it. Kothari focused his analysis on 'modern industrial civilisation' and the 'approach to science and technology' steering India's development, recalling the 1955 Russell-Einstein manifesto, which had declared that 'there lies before us, if we choose, continual progress in happiness, knowledge and wisdom.' Yet he argued that this promised new Paradise did not seem so clear two decades later; instead humanity faced injustices and inequities. He acknowledged modern science had done immense good by liberating people from the horrors of nature and religious doctrine, but under existing paradigms it was being used as 'an instrument of power and domination rather than as a liberator of the human spirit.' Employing an analysis familiar to today's degrowth advocates, Kothari wrote that the myth of perpetual progress had been busted: the claim that growth could be made 'infinite and unending and hence available to all' was deployed to convince the public it was possible. He warned instead of serious threats including 'the threat of total war, the threat of extreme deprivation coexisting with over-abundance, the threat of the collapse of the biosphere.' To Kothari and others, the primary cause was the 'acquisitive ethic' of modern living and a 'pursuit of a parasitic and wasteful style of life,' an ethic visible in everyday consumption such as owning 50 sarees. He grouped Global South elites with Western nations for embracing these wasteful lifestyles, arguing that within the South there existed domination not only by the North but also 'domination of large masses of the people by small, privileged, mainly urban-based and westernised, elites which are more closely tied to the metropolitan centres of the world than to their own peoples.' He concluded that a century of 'unprecedented material progress' had simultaneously been one of 'sprawling misery and increasing deprivation,' so the path forward required radical reimagining: land reforms redistributing available land for employment and minimum income, massive public works programmes to build durable community assets and restore local resource endowments, and encouragement of new small-scale industries producing goods for the general public. A major vehicle for this quest was the Indo-Dutch Programme for Alternatives in Development, whose memorandum ICSSR's Member-Secretary JP Naik signed in 1975. Naik also helped reimagine Indian healthcare through his role on the Srivastav Committee, which issued its report 'Health Services And Medical Education: A Programme For Immediate Action' in 1975; based on it India instituted its first nationwide community health workers network in 1977, anticipating ASHA workers by about 40 years. The committee argued that India had devoted disproportionately more resources to high-end hospitals and doctor training than local, community-based needs warranted. Quoting Naik: 'After 30 years of development of health services, we find ourselves in the position of a traveller who sets out on a long journey, and even before he has travelled about three-tenths of the distance to his goal, finds that his purse has been stolen, his car has developed serious trouble and grave doubts have arisen even about the correctness of the route he had decided to follow.' The article notes that very few proposals from this 1970s-80s intellectual ferment were taken seriously in power. It observes that Kothari's diagnosed acquisitive ethic and the paradox of deprivation coexisting with over-abundance have worsened, and that despite rhetorical attention to ASHA workers India has continued amplifying doctor-, hospital-, and technology-centric models. Recent environmental disasters in northern India's Himalayan region and Nepal's August flash flood disaster again catalysed calls for a 'fresh stock-taking, and a questioning of the capital-centric development model.' The author concludes by noting that elites offer only tiny tweaks to the political economy wheel while Kothari and others argue the real solution requires complete reinvention. Kiran Kumbhar is identified as historian of India, medicine, and public health based in the US.
items.title: India's 1970s 'Alternatives in Development' as a Prescient Critique of Growth-Centric Models

items.summary: On November 18, petrol and diesel prices remained largely unchanged across major Indian cities even as the Centre eliminated additional excise duty applicable to petrol exports. Domestic retailers continued shielding consumers from recent Middle East-driven oil price shocks by holding rates steady. Fuel costs vary between states due to local Value Added Tax (VAT), freight charges, and other localized factors. As of November 18, New Delhi had relatively lower prices at ₹102.12 per litre for petrol and ₹95.20 per litre for diesel. Mumbai stood at ₹111.21 per litre for petrol and ₹97.83 per litre for diesel. Chennai priced petrol at ₹107.76 per litre and diesel at ₹99.55 per litre. Kolkata was the highest among metros, with petrol at ₹113.51 per litre and diesel at ₹99.82 per litre. Bengaluru had petrol at ₹110.44 per litre and diesel at ₹99.56 per litre. Hyderabad carried the steepest prices overall: petrol at ₹116.15 per litre and diesel at ₹104.23 per litre. Union Minister Suresh Gopi stated that an immediate reduction in fuel prices was not technically possible, citing losses of ₹42,000 crore incurred by oil companies and chaos in the supply of petroleum products. He noted that while prices might fall "the next day," compensation for these losses must first be addressed, referring to the West Asia conflict. Separately, global crude prices fell on Wednesday after data showed an increase in US crude and fuel inventories during the week ended November 13. Crude stocks rose by 5.28 million barrels per market sources citing the American Petroleum Institute, while gasoline stocks increased by 5.12 million barrels and distillate inventories by 351,000 barrels. US West Texas Intermediate futures fell 56 cents, or 0.65%, to $85.45 a barrel as of 0149 GMT, while Brent crude futures declined 16 cents, or 0.17%, to $92.98 a barrel. However, continued tensions between the US and Iran and ongoing risks to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz limited these price declines.
items.title: Indian fuel prices steady on November 18 despite export duty cut and Middle East tensions

The article uses Fidel Castro's 2026 birth centenary (1926-2026) as a vantage point for examining post-Revolution Cuban cinema. It argues that no head of state did more than Castro to explore cinema both to chronicle the achievements of a new political order and to highlight areas where further work remained, with documentary at the centre while fiction laced with documentary also featured prominently.

Santiago Álvarez is presented as having been entrusted with making the world aware of the Bolshevik Revolution's relevance; he had gone to the US to make money but returned after witnessing capitalism up close. Among older-generation filmmakers, Tomás Alea worked across varied themes including Memories of Underdevelopment, Death of a Bureaucrat, Up to a Point, The Last Supper and Strawberry and Chocolate. Humberto Solás, who died of cancer on September 17, 2008, is identified chiefly with what he called 'historical melodramas' set within Cuban political, social, artistic and personal realities of the 20th century.

The article asserts that Cuba's filmmakers had to serve as the fledgling nation's conscience keepers. Solás joined ICAIC (Instituto Cubano del Arte e Industria Cinematográficos) in 1959 as a typist, having chosen urban guerrilla work over formal studies during what he described as an unstable time when Batista closed down universities or students did so themselves. He noted that early fiction shorts carried reflections of cultural inferiority and alienation felt even among gifted artists on the three colonised and neo-colonised continents awed by European and Western film styles, observing 'Neither me, nor my generation, nor my country can be seen in any of these films.' This realisation drove his turn to historical subjects; he argued Cuba lacked a coherent appreciation of its national past because history had been filtered through a bourgeois lens. In calling his films 'historical melodrama', Solás sought a Marxist perspective providing materialist interpretation of both events and individual psychology.

Solás, like Pastor Vega (Portrait of Teresa), frequently used women as central metaphor, believing dominated groups feel more deeply the contradictions in society; his critique of machismo in Lucia is cited as likely to remain a reference point for discussion. He said 'The sad masquerade of limited, archetyped, and suffocating human relations in defence of private property is most transparent in the case of women—half of humanity.' His Oscar-nominated Un hombre de éxito (A Successful Man) covered roughly 30 years, contrasting two brothers separated by ideology and ambition.

The article notes that Cuban directors remain visible as political thinkers because distribution channels are manipulated by North American distributors. Solás said 'Although the so-called Third World is heterogeneous, I can talk about the Latin American Cinemas,' identifying distribution as their greatest problem; he cited Cuba's Foundation of New Cinema in Latin America based in Havana and its aim to buy at least one theatre in every Latin American country.

On US hostility and sanctions, the article states that since February 1962 when John F. Kennedy imposed the first trade and economic sanctions, no president has been so consistently hostile as Donald Trump; it also notes right-wing nominees winning across Argentina, Chile, Bolivia, Peru, Colombia and Ecuador. Goran Radovanović's With Fidel Whatever Happens (2011), a 50-minute colour film set in Sierra Maestra about the day before the Revolution's 52nd anniversary, is presented as one cinematic reply.

The article describes the film as episodic, realistic with long- and mid-shots creating distance to guard against sentimentality. It features an old man repairing a motorcycle, a young dentist travelling by foot, donkey and bus (one patient improbably named Vladimir Ilyich Rodriguez), and a couple sharing their telephone with neighbours whose framed photograph suggests a lost child. Radovanović said 'The fate of these people...is depicted on a day of ideological ecstasy … And the following day? The next day, driven by inertia, they all return to the rhythm of everyday life which is the same and is not very promising.'

Finally, the article frames Cuba's struggle as one of the longest wars in history since January 1, 1959 (67 years), a conflict fought without bullets or bombs but with economic sanctions. The author, Vidyarthy Chatterjee, writes about cinema, society and politics; his most recent book is About Nothing in Particular.

The piece reads as advocacy for the Cuban Revolution rather than neutral reporting: it uses charged language ('rogue elephantine aggressor', 'fiendish'), frames US actions negatively without offering counter-perspective, and presents all claims about filmmakers' intentions and Cuba's resilience uncritically. It also contains editorializing beyond its stated subject (e.g., comparisons to Lenin/Stalin in India) that extends the argument rather than reporting on cinema.
items.title: Cuban cinema as revolutionary conscience: Solás, ICAIC and resistance to US sanctions

items.summary: This Hindustan Times morning brief, dated November 18, compiles key developments across India and the world. In Jammu and Kashmir, a fresh encounter between security forces and terrorists broke out in Kulgam district on Wednesday; most-wanted terrorist Lateef Bhat—who had escaped after his aide was killed earlier that week—is now trapped by forces and is believed to be the last active local commander in South Kashmir (South Valley). Separately, Chief Justice of India Surya Kant, consulting with the four most senior Supreme Court judges, has shifted at least two matters away from a bench headed by justice Ahsanuddin Amanullah over its decision to expand individual disputes into nationwide public interest litigations (PILs). In corporate news, Nvidia chairman Harvey Jones said on Tuesday that the board has no plans to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO, even though Huang expressed willingness to return if asked; he had stepped down last week following revelations about extramarital relationships, including an alleged affair with a woman suspected of having links to Chinese intelligence. On the cricket front, Chennai Super Kings announced on November 17 that MS Dhoni would take over as team mentor and close his playing career in the IPL, though he will remain with CSK; earlier discussion had centered on whether the franchise would retain his ₹4 crore contract or use it at the auction. In entertainment, Nitesh Tiwari's Ramayana—starring Ranbir Kapoor, Sai Pallavi and Yash—is a two-part adaptation of Valmiki's epic that has now crossed ₹820 crore in India; though its daily collections dipped during the second week as it felt the impact of an extended run, the film continues toward the ₹850 crore milestone. items.summary: A senior Municipal Corporation of Delhi (MCD) official told the Hindustan Times that a report on the time and resources required to conduct a door-to-door structural-safety survey has been sent to the central government. In response to a series of building collapses and fires in Delhi, the union home ministry directed MCD last month to prepare a roadmap for auditing fire and structural safety across every house and building in the capital, including authorised and unauthorised localities. The report states that at least four million man-hours are needed to survey all buildings citywide; with more than 40 lakh structures present, even one assessor per house taking an hour yields roughly 5,00,000 working days, or about 1,000 days if only 500 workers are deployed. Civic officials said the central government must decide whether such a survey is warranted and what timeline to follow, noting that it would involve filling out forms on building age, covered area, visible structural deficiencies, and absence of a fire NOC or building plan, after which policy could be shaped and the union government decides how to proceed. A scientific structural audit would be even more costly at Rs1-5 lakh per building depending on area; senior officials warn it is a mammoth exercise requiring substantial funding, manpower, and independent technical expertise that civic agencies currently lack. MCD's current annual dangerous-building survey covers around 3.25 million buildings using largely visual inspections to flag cracks and leaning walls, whereas the proposed home ministry audit would examine both structural integrity and fire safety; additionally, MCD lacks a dedicated unit for structural-safety audits and has no permanent structural engineers on its rolls, relying instead on 249 empanelled third-party engineers who would each have to assess more than 16,000 buildings if all four million structures were audited, or substantially more across the 7.6 million census houses; the home ministry is expected to decide whether MCD should hire a third-party agency or use architects already empanelled with civic bodies. In June 2020, following intervention by the Delhi High Court after the incorporation of seismic provisions in Delhi's building bye-laws, the three erstwhile municipal corporations set a six-month deadline for high-risk and older structures to obtain structural safety certificates; officials said that exercise could barely cover a few thousand buildings even after six years. The Tejendra Khanna Committee, established in 2006 to examine unauthorised construction and misuse of premises, estimated that 70-80% of structures had violated building norms, while Delhi falls under Seismic Zone IV (high earthquake risk); officials said any eventual audit would need to prioritise high-rise buildings, large assembly buildings, government offices, older properties, and other vulnerable structures. The item was written by Paras Singh, Deputy Metro Editor at Hindustan Times, who joined the paper in 2021 after beginning his career at The Times of India in 2016.

items.summary:
A Finshots piece evaluates what happened ten years after the November 2016 demonetisation, when Prime Minister Narendra Modi announced that ₹500 and ₹1,000 notes would no longer be legal tender. The author recalls watching the news break during dinner at home, with people lining up outside ATMs to withdraw ₹400 in cash because only ₹100 notes were available then; UPI had existed for barely three months but was not yet used widely. Notes worth about ₹15 lakh crore vanished overnight, and most of India's cash-dependent informal sector suffered as almost everything ran on scarce cash.

The article then examines each stated objective against the data. On black money: 99.3% of banned notes came back, with only about ₹10,720 crore missing; before the ban it was expected that roughly ₹4-5 lakh crore held as untaxed cash would not return, but this did not happen because people earning untaxed income often park wealth in real estate, gold or shell companies rather than keeping all of it as cash. The RBI board had also warned beforehand that demonetisation was unlikely to significantly impact black money and counterfeit notes.

On fake currency: the author disputes the claim linking cash-in-circulation magnitude directly to corruption levels, using Japan (a cleaner economy) with about 20% cash-to-GDP versus India's around 12%, which has stayed fairly stable despite UPI growth because GDP also grew and many transactions—real estate, weddings, tips, rural small-shop payments—still occur in cash. NPCI is planning a fee for UPI transactions above ₹2,000, which could push some shops back to cash. On counterfeits: RBI data shows counterfeit notes detected per crore fell from 70 in FY16 to 13 in FY26 overall; but focusing on the higher-denomination ₹500 note (where counterfeiting is most common), fakes rose from 0.3 to 20 per crore between demonetisation and now, though this uses only new notes so FY17 was a poor baseline. Comparing old versus current ₹500 notes instead shows counterfeits fell from about 167 to 20 per crore—suggesting the anti-counterfeit goal was largely met; yet fakes were never a huge problem as they formed a tiny fraction of total notes, and demonetisation cost an estimated 1.5-2% loss in economic output while hurting the informal sector.

On widening the tax net (an objective added later): filing returns jumped partly because cash deposits could now be traced to PAN records, but GST arrived in 2017 along with wider TDS use; new filers earned about ₹2.7 lakh on average, barely above the ₹2.5 lakh threshold at the time, and direct tax collections rose only slightly from 5.53% of GDP in FY17 to 5.86% the following year before falling to 4.78% by FY21, then reaching a high of 6.73% in FY25 after the pandemic.

The final verdict: demonetisation nudged people toward digital payments and brought more into the tax-filing system—though the pandemic was also a powerful force pushing contactless payments, which leave trails that can eventually expand the tax base—but curbing black money clearly failed; this would require stricter law enforcement and measures to plug loopholes letting people park undisclosed income in other assets or buy property with cash. The author ends by noting that until then… (an incomplete sentence). A Ditto term insurance advertisement follows, addressed to breadwinners about financial security if they are not around.

The article is a Finshots piece; the source text is marked untrusted.

items.summary: Acting US Navy Secretary Hung Cao acknowledged during his Senate Armed Services Committee confirmation hearing on Tuesday that the war with Iran was straining naval resources. Testifying before Senator Mazie Hirono of Hawaii to become the Navy's permanent secretary, Cao said 'it is stressing our naval resources.' He defended the military campaign, arguing that the combined performance of American forces demonstrated capabilities that would give China pause. Hirono challenged this assessment, noting that the concentration of naval forces in the Middle East was diverting ships and attention from the Indo-Pacific, where the United States faces challenges from China and North Korea. She said the conflict had consumed tens of billions of dollars, drawn down critical munitions, delayed maintenance, and forced sailors and their families to endure extended deployments. Hirono also questioned whether an emphasis on building more ships was being matched by investment in the shipyards needed to maintain them, arguing that longer deployments compounded the maintenance burden when vessels returned. Cao praised shipyard workers in Hawaii, saying some had been temporarily assigned to other yards to help address workforce shortages. He acknowledged the strain but argued that coordinated use of American naval, ground, air and cyber capabilities had unsettled China. Hirono rejected this interpretation, saying Beijing remained active in the Indo-Pacific as Washington concentrated on the Middle East. Cao responded that comparisons of ships and aircraft did not capture the strength of the US enlisted force, pointing to responsibilities entrusted to young sailors, including operating aircraft carriers and launching aircraft. When asked whether he had raised the war's impact on readiness with President Donald Trump and the defense secretary, Cao said he had laid out the Navy's requirements along with options, mitigation plans, and fallback arrangements. Separately, Senator Mark Kelly of Arizona pressed Cao about sailor welfare during extended Middle East deployments. Kelly cited eight suicide attempts across the USS Abraham Lincoln carrier strike group during a deployment lasting 321 days, and relayed family complaints about inadequate food, weight loss, and shortages of basic hygiene supplies on deployed vessels. Those accounts were presented by Kelly; Cao maintained that food supplies were adequate. Cao said he reviewed shipboard conditions and remaining rations daily, identifying the destroyer USS Gonzalez as a particular concern because it had about a week's supplies remaining, below the two weeks he preferred. Asked whether ships had run out of supplies, Cao said they had not. Kelly challenged Cao over a parent's report that a service member had lost more than 45 pounds in six months; Cao compared this to children finding an empty refrigerator, while Kelly argued such weight loss could not be explained simply by dissatisfaction with food choices. Kelly also challenged Cao's description of the eight suicide attempts as successful interventions. Cao pointed to chaplains, mental health specialists, and resilience counselors aboard ships, while Kelly acknowledged deaths had been prevented but said the Navy still needed to address conditions facing deployed personnel.
